title: Serving LLMs: Caching, Limits & Guardrails
summary: LLM calls are slow, metered per token, and full of user text. Learn the gateway layer that sits in front of a model: token-bucket rate limits, exact and semantic response caches, PII redaction with checksum validation, context-window truncation that never drops the system prompt, and cost accounting.
takeaways: A token bucket allows short bursts up to its capacity while enforcing an average rate. Cap the refill, or idle time turns into an unbounded burst.
Exact caches need normalized keys that include the generation params, plus a TTL so stale answers expire. Semantic caches trade a similarity threshold for hit rate.
Redact PII before it reaches logs or third-party models, and validate matches (Luhn for card numbers) so you don't mangle order IDs.
When a chat exceeds the context budget, keep the system prompt and drop the oldest turns. Count tokens and dollars per model so costs stay visible.

steps.label: Rate limit
steps.detail: Spend from the caller's token bucket. If it's empty, reject with 429 before doing any work.

steps.label: Redact
steps.detail: Replace emails, phone numbers and Luhn-valid card numbers with placeholders.

steps.label: Cache lookup
steps.detail: Exact key (normalized prompt + params) first, then the nearest embedding above the similarity threshold.

steps.label: Fit the context
steps.detail: Keep the system prompt and the most recent turns that fit the token budget.

steps.label: Call + account
steps.detail: Call the model, store the response with a timestamp, and record input and output tokens and cost.

terms.definition: A rate limiter holding up to `capacity` tokens that refill at a fixed rate. Each request spends tokens or is rejected.
Time to live: how long a cached entry stays valid before it must be recomputed.
When the cache is full, discard the least recently used entry first.
A cache that returns a stored response when a new prompt's embedding is within a cosine-similarity threshold of a cached prompt.
A mod-10 check digit scheme used by payment card numbers that catches every single-digit error and most adjacent transpositions.
Replacing personally identifiable information such as emails, phone numbers and card numbers with placeholders before storage or forwarding.
